# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, pinch flat risk and handling. The right number depends on rider weight, tire width, tire construction and the surface you ride on. Use the ranges below as starting points, then adjust by feel and by checking the sidewall rating.

## Before you start

Check the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Never exceed it. Measure with a gauge you trust, since many floor pumps read differently from each other. Set pressure when the tires are cold, and check again after the first few rides because latex and butyl tubes lose air over time.

Total rider plus bike weight matters more than rider weight alone. Carrying a loaded bag, a pack or a child seat adds load to the rear tire, so the rear pressure may need a small increase.

## Road bikes

Typical tire widths are 23 to 32 mm. Road tires usually run on smooth pavement, so the goal is low rolling resistance with enough cushion to avoid pinch flats and rough-road fatigue.

Starting points for a 700c road tire with a tube:

- 23 mm tires: about 100 to 115 psi (6.9 to 7.9 bar) for a rider around 70 kg.
- 25 mm tires: about 90 to 105 psi (6.2 to 7.2 bar) for the same rider.
- 28 mm tires: about 75 to 90 psi (5.2 to 6.2 bar).
- 32 mm tires: about 60 to 75 psi (4.1 to 5.2 bar).

Heavier riders should run the upper part of each range. Lighter riders can run lower. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same comfort and grip.

Tubeless road setups often run 5 to 10 psi lower than the tubed figure for the same tire width, because the tire can seal and conform without pinch flat risk. Confirm with your tire maker's guidance.

Road signs that pressure is too high: a harsh, bouncing ride, the bike skipping over small bumps, and reduced grip in corners. Signs that it is too low: a squirming feel in fast corners, a soft tire that rubs the rim on hard impacts, and frequent pinch flats.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide, and some run wider. They spend time on loose dirt, gravel, mud and pavement in one ride, so the pressure should balance traction with puncture protection.

Starting points for tubeless gravel tires:

- 35 mm tires: about 32 to 38 psi (2.2 to 2.6 bar) for a rider around 70 kg.
- 40 mm tires: about 28 to 34 psi (1.9 to 2.3 bar).
- 45 mm tires: about 24 to 30 psi (1.7 to 2.1 bar).
- 50 mm tires: about 22 to 27 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar).

For tubed gravel tires, add 3 to 5 psi to these figures, since tubes are more prone to pinch flats at low pressure.

Move toward the lower end of a range for loose, sandy or rough terrain, and toward the higher end for smooth hardpack, long road sections or heavy loads. A quick test is to ride a short loop and check whether the tire squirms in turns or the rim hits on impacts. If it does, add a little air. If the bike feels harsh and skittish, let a little air out.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.0 to 2.6 inches wide, with the widest options used for trail and enduro riding. Most ride tubeless. Pressure controls traction on roots, rock and loose corners, and also controls how well the tire absorbs impacts.

Starting points for tubeless mountain tires:

- Cross-country, 2.0 to 2.2 inch tires: about 26 to 30 psi (1.8 to 2.1 bar) for a rider around 70 kg.
- Trail, 2.3 to 2.4 inch tires: about 23 to 27 psi (1.6 to 1.9 bar).
- Enduro or downhill, 2.4 to 2.6 inch tires: about 20 to 25 psi (1.4 to 1.7 bar).

Raise the pressure for heavier riders, for hardpack and for fast rolling trails. Lower it for wet, loose or rocky terrain where grip matters most. Many riders set the front tire 1 to 3 psi lower than the rear, because the front steers and brakes more.

If you hit the rim on roots or drops, or the tire burps air off the bead in corners, the pressure is too low for the terrain. If the bike bounces off the trail and loses grip over small bumps, the pressure is too high.

## Quick reference

| Bike type | Typical width | Common pressure range | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| Road, tubed | 23 to 28 mm | 75 to 115 psi | 5.2 to 7.9 bar |
| Gravel, tubeless | 35 to 45 mm | 24 to 38 psi | 1.7 to 2.6 bar |
| Mountain, tubeless | 2.3 to 2.6 in | 20 to 30 psi | 1.4 to 2.1 bar |

The ranges assume a rider near 70 kg. Scale them up about 2 to 3 percent for each 5 kg above that weight, and down by the same amount for each 5 kg below.

## Testing your setup

Start in the middle of the range. Ride the same loop at two pressures, one 2 psi lower and one 2 psi higher, and note which feels faster, more stable and more comfortable on your terrain. Change one thing at a time. Keep a note of the figures that work for each wheel set, since a change of tire or rim width shifts the right number.

# Tire Pressure Guide

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, and flat risk. Start from the ranges below, then adjust for rider weight, tire width, and tire construction. Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.

## Before you start

Check pressure when the tires are cold, either before the first ride of the day or several hours after riding. Use a gauge you trust. Gauges built into floor pumps can be off by several psi, so a separate gauge helps. Read the pressure at the valve and make sure the bead is seated evenly before you read it.

## Road bikes

Common road tire widths are 25c to 32c. These are starting points for a rider around 75 kg (165 lb):

* 23c: about 100 to 115 psi
* 25c: about 90 to 105 psi
* 28c: about 80 to 95 psi
* 32c: about 70 to 85 psi

Wider tires run at lower pressure and grip better on rough chip seal and broken pavement. A hard tire bounces over bumps and loses traction. On wet roads, drop about 5 psi from your dry setting, staying inside the tire's range. Tubeless road tires often run 5 to 10 psi lower than tube versions of the same width.

## Gravel bikes

Common gravel tire widths are 35c to 50c, often run tubeless. These are starting points for a rider around 75 kg:

* 35c: about 35 to 42 psi
* 40c: about 30 to 38 psi
* 45c: about 27 to 34 psi
* 50c: about 25 to 30 psi

On smooth hardpack, run the higher end. On loose gravel, dirt roads, or washboard, run lower. With tubeless tires and sealant, you can run lower pressures safely. With tubes, stay higher to avoid pinch flats and rim strikes. Heavy loads call for a few psi more.

## Mountain bikes

Common mountain bike widths are 2.2 to 2.6 inches, usually run tubeless. These are starting points for a rider around 75 kg:

* 2.2 inch trail tires: about 25 to 30 psi
* 2.3 to 2.4 inch tires: about 22 to 27 psi
* 2.5 to 2.6 inch tires: about 20 to 25 psi

On wet, loose, or rooty trails, run lower for more grip and better bump absorption. On hardpack and fast, rocky descents, run slightly higher to reduce pinch-flat risk. Many riders run the front tire a few psi lower than the rear. Hardtail riders often find that difference useful. On full suspension bikes, follow the bike maker's recommendation and the tire maker's minimum.

## Adjusting for rider weight

The ranges above assume a rider around 75 kg. Heavier riders need more pressure, and lighter riders need less. As a rough guide, move the number by a few psi for every 10 kg away from 75 kg. Treat every figure in this guide as a starting point, then fine tune by feel.

## Signs the pressure is wrong

Too low: the tire squirms in corners, the tire feels soft and mushy, the rim hits the ground on bumps (causing a pinch flat or dent), and the tire may roll slower on hard, smooth surfaces.

Too high: the ride feels harsh, the bike skips over bumps, grip drops on rough surfaces, and the tire can feel like it is rattling.

## Tubeless and tubes

Tubeless tires seal with liquid sealant and resist pinch flats, so they can run lower pressures. Sealant dries out over time, so refresh it every few months. Tubed tires need pressure kept within range, because pinch flats are much more likely when pressure falls below the minimum.

## Routine

Check pressure before every ride. Butyl tubes typically lose about 1 to 2 psi per day, and some tires lose more. Recheck after changing tires, because a new tubeless tire can lose pressure while it seats and settles.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

These figures are starting points. Adjust them to your weight, terrain, tire construction and comfort. Always stay inside the minimum and maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.

## Why pressure matters

Pressure controls grip, rolling resistance, comfort and pinch-flat risk. Low pressure gives more grip and comfort but raises the chance of a pinch flat or rim damage. High pressure rolls faster on smooth surfaces but skips over loose or rough ground and feels harsh.

Two factors set the right number more than any other: how much you weigh (rider plus bike and gear), and how wide the tire is. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same load because the contact patch is larger.

## Measuring

- Use a gauge you trust. Gas station gauges often read high or low.
- Check pressure cold, before riding. Pressure rises a few psi as tires heat up.
- Expect small losses over days. Latex tubes and some tubeless setups lose air faster than butyl tubes.
- Pressure is reported in psi (pounds per square inch) or bar. 1 bar is about 14.5 psi.

## Road bikes

Typical tire widths are 23 to 28 mm. Road tires have smooth tread and run at high pressure.

Starting pressures for a rider and bike totaling about 75 kg (165 lb), with tubes:

| Tire width | Pressure (psi) | Pressure (bar) |
|---|---|---|
| 23 mm | 100 to 115 | 6.9 to 7.9 |
| 25 mm | 90 to 105 | 6.2 to 7.2 |
| 28 mm | 80 to 95 | 5.5 to 6.5 |

Adjustments:

- Heavier total load: add about 5 psi for each 10 kg above 75 kg.
- Lighter total load: reduce by a similar amount.
- Tubeless: run 5 to 10 psi lower than the tube figure for the same width, which improves grip and reduces pinch-flat risk.
- Wet or rough roads: drop 5 psi and consider a wider tire.
- Race days on smooth pavement: the upper end of the range is fine.

Use the tire's maximum pressure as a ceiling, not a target. Many road tires are rated to 120 psi or more, but that is rarely the best setting.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide with a mix of smooth and knobby tread. Pressure is the biggest lever on gravel, because it changes comfort, traction and flat risk together.

Starting pressures for a rider and bike totaling about 75 kg (165 lb), tubeless:

| Tire width | Pressure (psi) | Pressure (bar) |
|---|---|---|
| 35 mm | 35 to 40 | 2.4 to 2.8 |
| 40 mm | 30 to 36 | 2.1 to 2.5 |
| 45 mm | 26 to 32 | 1.8 to 2.2 |
| 50 mm | 24 to 28 | 1.7 to 1.9 |

With tubes, add about 5 psi to these numbers, because tubes need more pressure to avoid pinch flats.

Adjustments:

- Smooth gravel or fast roads: use the higher end.
- Loose, washboard or rocky terrain: use the lower end. Lower pressure absorbs bumps and keeps the tire from bouncing off the surface.
- Heavier load, such as bikepacking bags: add 2 to 4 psi.
- Front and rear: many riders run the front 1 to 3 psi lower than the rear, because the front carries less weight but steers and brakes.

Gravel tubeless setups are the most common approach. They allow lower pressure without pinch flats, but check that the tire and rim are a tubeless-compatible pair and that the bead is seated fully.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain tires run 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, with aggressive tread and often tubeless. Pressure is set low to maximize grip, traction and suspension performance.

Starting pressures for a rider and bike totaling about 75 kg (165 lb), tubeless:

| Tire width | Pressure (psi) | Pressure (bar) |
|---|---|---|
| 2.2 in, cross-country | 25 to 30 | 1.7 to 2.1 |
| 2.3 to 2.4 in, trail | 22 to 27 | 1.5 to 1.9 |
| 2.5 to 2.6 in, enduro or downhill | 20 to 24 | 1.4 to 1.7 |

Adjustments:

- Heavier rider: add 1 to 3 psi.
- Rocky, rooty or steep terrain: lower the pressure by 1 to 3 psi for more grip and less rim impact.
- Hardpack or fast smooth trails: raise it by 1 to 2 psi to reduce rolling resistance.
- Front and rear: the front is often 1 to 2 psi lower than the rear, since it carries more of the braking load on descents. Some riders run the same pressure front and rear.
- Hardtail bikes without suspension: ride a little higher than a full-suspension bike, because the tires carry all the impact.

Run too low and the tire can roll off the rim in corners or burp air through the bead. Run too high and the bike skates, loses traction and jars your hands.

## Common mistakes

- Setting pressure by feel alone. Use a gauge and record your settings until you know what works.
- Ignoring the sidewall rating. Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the tire.
- Setting pressure with the wheel hot, after a long ride or in the sun.
- Changing pressure to fix a handling problem that is really caused by suspension setup, tire choice or saddle position.

## Quick reference

- Road, 25 mm, 75 kg: about 95 psi with tubes, 85 psi tubeless.
- Gravel, 40 mm, 75 kg: about 33 psi tubeless.
- Mountain, 2.4 in, 75 kg: about 25 psi tubeless.

For each figure, change one setting at a time, ride the same loop, and note how the bike feels before you change it again.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

These are starting points. Your ideal pressure depends on your weight, the tire width, the rim width, whether the tires are tubeless, and the terrain. Adjust in small steps of 1 to 2 psi and note what feels best.

## Why pressure matters

Pressure controls three things: grip, rolling resistance, and protection from pinch flats. Too little pressure makes the tire squirm in corners and can cause the rim to strike the ground or the tire to roll off the rim. Too much pressure reduces grip, transmits more bumps to you, and raises the risk of pinch flats on rough surfaces.

## General rules that apply to all bikes

- Heavier riders need more pressure. Heavier riders and loaded bikes should run higher pressures than lighter riders on the same tire.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure. A wide tire carries the same load over a larger contact patch, so it needs less air.
- Wider rims support wider tires. Check that your tire width suits your rim width.
- Tubeless setups run about 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed setups with the same tire, because the tire seals well and resists pinch flats.
- Hotter conditions raise pressure. Air expands as the tire warms, so inflate in the shade or at the temperature you will ride in.
- Use a gauge. Pumps with built-in gauges vary, so a separate gauge gives more consistent readings.
- Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.

## Road bikes

Road tires are narrow, usually 23 to 32 mm, and run at high pressure on smooth pavement. Rolling resistance drops as pressure rises on smooth surfaces, but comfort and grip suffer on rough roads.

Approximate starting points for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb), tubed:

- 23 mm tire: 95 to 110 psi
- 25 mm tire: 85 to 100 psi
- 28 mm tire: 75 to 90 psi
- 30 to 32 mm tire: 65 to 80 psi

Adjust by about 5 psi for every 10 kg of body weight above or below 70 kg. Tubeless road tires can run about 5 psi lower than the same tire tubed.

Signs the pressure is too high: a harsh ride, the bike bouncing over small cracks, and reduced grip in wet corners. Signs it is too low: the tire feels squishy when cornering, a soft rolling feel with noticeable tire squirm, or rim strikes on bumps.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide and run lower than road tires. The goal is traction and comfort on loose, mixed surfaces, with enough pressure to avoid pinch flats and rim damage.

Approximate starting points for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb):

- 35 to 38 mm tire, tubed: 40 to 50 psi
- 38 to 42 mm tire, tubed: 35 to 45 psi
- 40 to 45 mm tire, tubeless: 25 to 35 psi
- 45 to 50 mm tire, tubeless: 22 to 30 psi

For rough, rocky, or muddy routes, go toward the lower end of these ranges. For smooth gravel or a heavier bike and rider, go toward the higher end. Remember to adjust for body weight as described above.

Signs the pressure is too high: the bike skips or bounces on loose gravel and the tire loses traction. Signs it is too low: the tire feels squirmy in corners, the tire sidewall rolls, or the rim hits the ground on sharp impacts. Tubeless setups are much less prone to pinch flats, so they can run lower with less risk.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are wide, typically 2.2 to 2.6 inches, and run at low pressure. Low pressure increases the contact patch for grip on roots, rock, and loose dirt, and it lets the tire absorb impacts. Most mountain bike riders run tubeless.

Approximate starting points for a rider around 75 kg (165 lb), tubeless:

- 2.2 to 2.3 inch tire, cross-country riding: 25 to 30 psi
- 2.3 to 2.4 inch tire, trail riding: 22 to 27 psi
- 2.4 to 2.6 inch tire, enduro or downhill: 20 to 25 psi

Run the front tire 2 to 3 psi lower than the rear. The front carries less weight but handles most steering and braking traction, so it benefits from a softer feel. Heavier riders, or riders who ride aggressively, need the higher end of each range.

To fine tune, ride a loop and watch for these signs. Too high: the bike skips over roots, grip is poor, and the ride feels harsh. Too low: the tire rolls or squirms in corners, you hear rim contact on impacts, or the tire burps air from the bead.

## Quick checklist

1. Check the sidewall maximum before you start.
2. Set pressure with a gauge, cold, at the temperature you will ride in.
3. Start from the middle of the range for your tire width and body weight.
4. Ride a short loop and make one change at a time.
5. Recheck pressure before each ride, since tires lose air over time, especially tubeless tires.

The numbers above are general guidance, not a substitute for the tire maker's recommendations. When in doubt, start at the higher end and lower the pressure gradually until the bike feels right and you do not get pinch flats or rim strikes.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, pinch flat risk and handling. The right pressure depends on rider weight, tire width, terrain, and whether the tire is tubeless. Treat the numbers below as starting points and adjust by feel.

## Core principles

- Pressure is a trade-off. Lower pressure gives more grip and comfort but more rolling resistance and a higher risk of pinch flats or rim damage. Higher pressure rolls faster on smooth surfaces but grips less and transmits more vibration.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same feel. A 30 mm tire needs more pressure than a 40 mm tire carrying the same load, because the wider tire spreads the load over more contact area and gives more volume per psi.
- Heavier riders need more pressure. Total system weight (rider, bike, luggage, water) is what matters.
- Tubeless tires can run about 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed tires with the same width, because the sealant and the absence of an inner tube reduce pinch flat risk.
- Always check the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Do not exceed it. Rim maximum pressure, if printed on the rim, also applies.
- Measure pressure with a gauge. Pumps with built-in gauges can read off by several psi. Check pressure cold, before riding, and again after a ride because tires lose pressure over time.
- Temperature changes pressure. Pressure drops roughly 1 psi for every 10 degrees F (about 1 psi for every 5.5 degrees C) of cooling.

## Road bikes

### Typical range

Most road tires are 23 to 32 mm wide and run 80 to 120 psi (5.5 to 8.3 bar). Wider road tires (28 to 32 mm) run lower than narrow ones (23 to 25 mm).

### Starting points by rider weight (tubed, 25 mm tires)

| Rider plus bike weight | Starting pressure |
|---|---|
| Under 130 lb (59 kg) | 85 to 95 psi |
| 130 to 165 lb (59 to 75 kg) | 95 to 105 psi |
| 165 to 200 lb (75 to 91 kg) | 105 to 115 psi |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 115 to 120 psi, or follow the tire maximum |

For 28 to 32 mm tires, drop about 5 to 10 psi from these numbers. Tubeless setups can drop a further 3 to 5 psi.

### Riding conditions

- Smooth pavement and racing: the upper end of the range.
- Rough chip seal or broken pavement: drop 5 to 10 psi for comfort and grip.
- Wet roads: drop 3 to 5 psi for more grip. Wet painted lines and manhole covers are slippery at any pressure.

### Signs of wrong pressure

- Too high: the bike feels harsh, the tire bounces over small bumps, and grip on corners feels light.
- Too low: the tire squirms in corners, the rim may hit the road on hard impacts (pinch flats), and rolling feels sluggish.

## Gravel bikes

### Typical range

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. They run much lower than road tires, often 30 to 50 psi (2 to 3.5 bar) depending on width, rider weight, and surface.

### Starting points by rider weight (tubeless, 40 mm tires)

| Rider plus bike weight | Starting pressure |
|---|---|
| Under 130 lb (59 kg) | 30 to 35 psi |
| 130 to 165 lb (59 to 75 kg) | 35 to 40 psi |
| 165 to 200 lb (75 to 91 kg) | 40 to 45 psi |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 45 to 50 psi |

For tubed tires, add about 3 to 5 psi. For 35 mm tires, add about 2 to 3 psi. For 45 to 50 mm tires, subtract about 2 to 3 psi.

### Riding conditions

- Smooth gravel and fast road sections: go higher within the range for speed.
- Loose, corrugated or rocky gravel: go lower for grip and comfort.
- Mud or sand: go lower still, but watch for rim strikes and tire roll-off.
- Long rides with luggage: add pressure to handle the extra load.

### Signs of wrong pressure

- Too high: the bike chatters over washboard and the tire skips on loose corners.
- Too low: the tire squirms, the tire may roll off the rim in hard corners (especially tubeless), and pinch flats are likely on rocks.

## Mountain bikes

### Typical range

Mountain bike tires are commonly 2.0 to 2.6 inches wide. Most run 18 to 30 psi (1.2 to 2.1 bar). Wider and softer casings run lower. Enduro and downhill tires may run lower still with heavy casings and inserts.

### Starting points by rider weight (tubeless, 2.3 to 2.4 inch tires)

| Rider plus bike weight | Starting pressure |
|---|---|
| Under 130 lb (59 kg) | 20 to 23 psi |
| 130 to 165 lb (59 to 75 kg) | 22 to 25 psi |
| 165 to 200 lb (75 to 91 kg) | 24 to 27 psi |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 26 to 30 psi |

For tubed tires, add about 5 psi. For 2.6 inch or wider tires, subtract 2 to 3 psi. For 2.0 to 2.2 inch tires, add 2 to 3 psi. For enduro or downhill riding with inserts, use the low end of the range or lower, and check the tire maximum.

### Riding conditions

- Hardpack and fast trails: higher end, for less rolling resistance.
- Roots, rock gardens and loose corners: lower end, for traction and to absorb impacts.
- Wet or muddy trails: lower end. Mud often needs a larger tread and lower pressure.
- Hard jumps and drops: a little more pressure reduces the chance of bottoming out, but stay within the rim and tire limits.

### Signs of wrong pressure

- Too high: the bike skips off roots, the tire feels hard, and traction on corners drops.
- Too low: the tire rolls off the rim, the wheel feels mushy and wallows, and rim dents or flats become likely.

## Setting pressure step by step

1. Check the tire sidewall for the maximum pressure and tire width.
2. Start from the table for your bike type and rider weight.
3. Set pressure with the bike in its riding setup, including any gear you carry.
4. Ride a short loop on your usual surface.
5. Adjust in steps of 1 to 2 psi. Lower for more grip and comfort, raise for more speed and less squirm.
6. Record the pressure that works for each surface so you can repeat it.

## Quick reference

- Road: 80 to 120 psi, narrow and high, wide and lower.
- Gravel: 30 to 50 psi, tubeless usually lower than tubed.
- Mountain: 18 to 30 psi, lower on rough or wet trails.
- Always stay within the maximum printed on the tire and rim.

These numbers are starting points. Always stay within the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall, and adjust to your weight, the surface, and how the bike feels.

## How to think about tire pressure

Pressure controls grip, rolling speed, comfort, and pinch flat risk. Lower pressure gives more contact patch and grip, and absorbs bumps. Higher pressure rolls faster on smooth pavement but transmits more vibration and can pinch flat on rough ground.

Three things set your starting pressure:

1. Rider and load weight. Heavier riders need more pressure to support the same tire.
2. Tire width. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same support.
3. Surface. Rough, loose, or wet ground calls for lower pressure.

Tubeless tires can run about 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed tires of the same size, because the bead seals against the rim and the tire does not need as much pressure to stay seated and to resist pinch flats.

Use a gauge. Pumps at gas stations and many floor pumps read inaccurately.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Typical pressures for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb):

- 23 mm: about 100 to 120 psi
- 25 mm: about 90 to 110 psi
- 28 mm: about 80 to 100 psi
- 32 mm: about 70 to 90 psi

Rules of thumb:

- Heavier riders should add pressure. Lighter riders can run lower.
- Wet roads, rough chip seal, or cobbles favor the lower end of the range.
- Smooth, dry tarmac and racing efforts favor the higher end.
- Wider tires at lower pressure often roll as fast as narrow tires at high pressure, and they feel more comfortable and grip better.

Road tires have no tread, so pressure matters a lot for cornering grip. If the tire squirms in corners, drop 5 psi.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Typical starting pressures for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb), tubed:

- 35 mm: about 40 to 50 psi
- 38 mm: about 35 to 45 psi
- 40 to 45 mm: about 30 to 40 psi
- 50 mm: about 25 to 35 psi

Tubeless setups usually run 3 to 5 psi lower than these figures.

Rules of thumb:

- Smooth gravel and hardpacked roads: use the higher end.
- Loose gravel, washboard, or long climbs with loose surfaces: use the lower end.
- Pinch flats on rough gravel usually mean the pressure is too low. Raise it 2 to 3 psi.
- Loose, squirmy handling or a tire that bottoms out on bumps means the pressure is too low.
- A harsh, bouncy ride with poor grip means the pressure is too high.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, and mountain bike pressure is the most sensitive to rider weight and terrain. Typical starting pressures, tubed, for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb):

- Cross country, 2.2 inch: about 28 to 32 psi front, 30 to 34 psi rear
- Trail, 2.3 to 2.4 inch: about 24 to 28 psi front, 26 to 30 psi rear
- Enduro and downhill, 2.4 to 2.6 inch: about 20 to 25 psi front, 22 to 27 psi rear

Tubeless setups usually run 2 to 4 psi lower than these figures.

Rules of thumb:

- The rear tire carries more weight on most bikes, so it usually runs a few psi higher than the front.
- Heavier riders add pressure. Lighter riders can drop it.
- Rocky, rooty, or fast descents call for lower pressure for grip and to absorb hits.
- Pinch flats or dents in the rim mean the pressure is too low for the terrain or the hit.
- Hard, skidding tires with little grip mean the pressure is too high.

Fat bikes with tires 3.8 inches or wider run much lower, often around 5 to 12 psi, depending on rider weight and snow or sand conditions.

## Quick check

1. Find the sidewall maximum and never exceed it.
2. Set pressure with a gauge, cold, before riding.
3. Ride 10 to 20 minutes on the surface you usually ride. Note grip, pinch flats, and comfort.
4. Change pressure in steps of 2 to 3 psi until the ride feels right.
5. Check pressure again every few rides. Tires lose a few psi per week, and tubeless setups lose more slowly than tubed ones.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

The pressures below are starting points. Adjust them to your body weight, tire width, rim width, terrain and whether the tires are tubeless. Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.

## Why pressure matters

Pressure controls three things: rolling resistance, grip and comfort. Too little pressure makes the tire squirm, raises rolling drag, and risks pinch flats on tubed wheels and rim strikes on any wheel. Too much pressure reduces grip and passes more shock into your hands, seat and feet. The best pressure is the lowest one that stays stable and does not bottom out or pinch flat on your usual surfaces.

## Factors that change the number

Body weight: Heavier riders need more pressure to support the same load. Rider plus bike plus cargo is the number that matters.

Tire width: Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same load because the contact patch is larger.

Rim width: A wider rim spreads the tire into a wider shape, which lowers the pressure you need for the same tire width. Check the rim width against the tire width chart from the rim maker.

Tubeless or tube: Tubeless tires can run 5 to 10 psi lower than tubed tires at the same size because a tube does not pinch between rim and ground.

Surface and conditions: Wet, loose or rough surfaces call for lower pressure. Smooth, dry pavement calls for higher pressure.

## Road bikes

Typical tire widths are 25 to 32 mm. Road bikes are the most sensitive to pressure, because a few psi changes how fast the bike rolls and how it feels.

Starting ranges for tubed or tubeless 25 mm tires:

1. Riders under about 130 lb (60 kg): 75 to 90 psi.
2. Riders about 130 to 160 lb (60 to 73 kg): 85 to 100 psi.
3. Riders about 160 to 190 lb (73 to 86 kg): 95 to 110 psi.

For 28 mm tires, drop each range by about 5 to 10 psi. For 32 mm tires, drop by about 10 to 15 psi. Tubeless setups can run a few psi lower than these numbers.

Road tips: Check pressure before every ride, because butyl tubes lose roughly 1 to 2 psi per day. Avoid pumping to the sidewall maximum unless you are a heavy rider on smooth roads. Start in the middle of the range and adjust by 3 to 5 psi on each ride until the bike feels fast and stable on rough patches.

## Gravel bikes

Typical tire widths are 35 to 50 mm. Gravel riding mixes pavement, dirt and loose surfaces, so pressure choice is a trade between speed and traction.

Starting ranges for tubeless 40 mm tires on a 20 to 25 mm internal width rim:

1. Riders under about 150 lb (68 kg): 30 to 38 psi.
2. Riders about 150 to 180 lb (68 to 82 kg): 35 to 43 psi.
3. Riders over about 180 lb (82 kg): 40 to 48 psi.

For smooth gravel or mostly pavement, use the upper end of the range. For loose, sandy or muddy gravel, use the lower end. Tubed tires need about 5 to 8 psi more than tubeless tires at the same setting.

Gravel tips: Note the pressure that gives good grip on your roughest route, then use the same setting on the next ride. Carry a small pump or CO2 inflator, and check the rim tape and sealant if a tubeless tire loses air.

## Mountain bikes

Typical tire widths are 2.2 to 2.6 inches (about 56 to 66 mm), and tubeless is the norm. Mountain bike pressure is the lowest of the three types, because the goal is traction and shock absorption on rough trails.

Starting ranges for tubeless 2.3 to 2.5 inch tires on a 30 mm internal width rim:

1. Riders under about 150 lb (68 kg): 20 to 24 psi.
2. Riders about 150 to 180 lb (68 to 82 kg): 22 to 27 psi.
3. Riders over about 180 lb (82 kg): 25 to 30 psi.

Run the front tire 1 to 3 psi lower than the rear, because the front carries less weight under braking. Wet roots, loose rock and steep descents call for lower pressure. Hardpack and fast flat trails call for higher pressure.

Mountain tips: Watch for rim strikes, which show up as dents or sudden flats, and raise pressure by 1 to 2 psi if they happen. Fork and shock settings are separate from tire pressure. Set sag on the suspension first, then tune the tires.

## Measuring and checking

Use a gauge you trust. Digital gauges and pump gauges can differ by several psi, so compare yours against a second gauge once. Measure cold, before riding, because pressure rises as tires warm up. Check the sidewall for the maximum and minimum pressure for each tire.

## Quick reference

Road, 25 mm: about 75 to 110 psi depending on rider weight.
Gravel, 40 mm tubeless: about 30 to 48 psi depending on rider weight.
Mountain, 2.3 to 2.5 inch tubeless: about 20 to 30 psi depending on rider weight, with the front 1 to 3 psi lower.

These ranges are general guidance. If a tire is new to you, start in the middle of the range and adjust from there.

# Tire Pressure Guide

These figures are starting points. Always stay below the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall, and adjust by feel after a few rides.

## Principles that apply to every bike

Pressure depends on four things: total weight (rider, bike, and gear), tire width, rim internal width, and terrain. A heavier rider needs more pressure. A wider tire runs at lower pressure for the same grip and comfort. A wider rim spreads the tire out, so it also runs slightly lower.

Check pressure cold, before riding. Pressure rises about 1 psi for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit of warming, so a tire pumped in a cold garage reads low on a hot afternoon. Use a digital or dial gauge rather than judging by squeeze.

Use a rim width and tire width chart from the rim maker when available. Tubeless setups can run 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed setups at the same width, because sealant and a tubeless bead hold the tire well at low pressure.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Pressure is the highest of the three types because the surface is smooth and rolling resistance drops with more pressure.

Starting points for a 70 kg (155 lb) rider on a typical road rim:

* 23 mm: about 95 to 110 psi
* 25 mm: about 85 to 100 psi
* 28 mm: about 75 to 90 psi
* 32 mm: about 65 to 80 psi

For a rider over 85 kg (185 lb), add about 5 to 10 psi. For a rider under 60 kg (130 lb), subtract about 5 psi. Wet roads, rough chip seal, or cobbled sections call for the lower end of the range or a wider tire.

Tubeless road tires commonly run 5 psi lower than the same tire in a tube.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Lower pressure gives grip on loose surfaces and reduces pinch flats on rocky roads.

Starting points for a 75 kg (165 lb) rider, tubeless on a 25 to 30 mm internal rim:

* 35 mm: about 32 to 36 psi
* 38 mm: about 29 to 33 psi
* 42 mm: about 26 to 30 psi
* 47 mm to 50 mm: about 22 to 27 psi

In a tube, go 3 to 5 psi higher than these tubeless numbers. On loose gravel, descents, or wet clay, drop 2 to 4 psi. On hard packed or paved routes, add 2 to 3 psi to reduce rolling resistance. If the tire rolls off the rim in corners, the pressure is too low for the load.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain tires are usually 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, tubeless in most cases. Pressure controls traction, cornering, and how much the tire absorbs impacts. Low pressure gives more grip but raises the risk of pinch flats and rim damage.

Starting points for a 75 kg (165 lb) rider, tubeless, 30 mm internal rim:

* Cross country, 2.2 inch tires: front about 25 psi, rear about 27 psi
* Trail, 2.4 inch tires: front about 23 psi, rear about 25 psi
* Enduro or downhill, 2.5 to 2.6 inch tires: front about 20 to 22 psi, rear about 22 to 24 psi

Run the rear about 2 psi higher than the front because the rear carries less weight on most bikes. Heavier riders add about 1 to 2 psi per 10 kg. On wet, rooty, or rocky trails, drop 1 to 3 psi. On hardpack or fast flow trails, add 1 to 2 psi.

If you ride a tube, go 3 to 5 psi higher to avoid pinch flats. Suspension sag is set separately, and tire pressure does not replace suspension setup.

## Quick reference

Road: 23 to 32 mm tires, 65 to 110 psi. Highest pressure, for smooth surfaces.

Gravel: 35 to 50 mm tires, 22 to 36 psi. Lower pressure for grip. Tubeless recommended.

Mountain: 2.2 to 2.6 inch tires, 20 to 27 psi. Lowest pressure. Tubeless recommended.

## Safety notes

Never exceed the sidewall maximum. Inspect the tire for cuts, bulges, or cracks before inflating. If a tire feels squirmy, bottoms out on the rim, or rolls off in a turn, add pressure in small steps. Record what works for your rider weight, tire, and terrain, then reuse those numbers.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, and the chance of a pinch flat. The right number depends on rider weight, tire width, tire casing, terrain, and whether the tire is tubed or tubeless. Always check the pressure range printed on the tire sidewall first. Never exceed the maximum.

## Basics that apply to all bikes

- Pressure is measured in PSI (pounds per square inch) or bar. 1 bar is about 14.5 PSI.
- Use a gauge. Pumps with built-in gauges can read 5 to 10 PSI off, so check with a separate gauge when accuracy matters.
- Check pressure cold, before riding. Tires lose about 1 to 2 PSI per week through the tube or tire, and warm tires read higher after a ride.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure than narrow tires at the same load. Pressure and width work together.
- Heavier riders, or riders carrying packs or panniers, need more pressure.
- Wet, slick, or loose surfaces call for lower pressure for more contact patch and grip.

## Road bikes

Road tires are narrow, usually 23 to 32 mm, and run at high pressure. The main goals are low rolling resistance and a smooth ride on paved surfaces.

A common starting point for a 70 kg (155 lb) rider:

- 23 mm tires: about 100 to 110 PSI (6.9 to 7.6 bar)
- 25 mm tires: about 90 to 100 PSI (6.2 to 6.9 bar)
- 28 mm tires: about 80 to 90 PSI (5.5 to 6.2 bar)
- 32 mm tires: about 65 to 80 PSI (4.5 to 5.5 bar)

Adjust by rider weight. Add about 5 PSI for each 10 kg above 70 kg, and subtract about 5 PSI for each 10 kg below it. Wider tires and rougher roads both justify dropping 5 to 10 PSI from these figures.

Signs the pressure is too high: a harsh, bouncy ride, rim strikes on bumps, and reduced grip in corners. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms in corners, feels soft on pedaling, or the rim contacts the road on hard hits. Pinch flats become more likely at low pressure on rough roads.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are typically 35 to 50 mm wide. Lower pressure gives grip on loose dirt, gravel, and mixed pavement, and it absorbs vibration on long rides.

A common starting point for a 70 kg (155 lb) rider:

- 35 mm tires: about 45 to 55 PSI (3.1 to 3.8 bar)
- 40 mm tires: about 40 to 50 PSI (2.8 to 3.4 bar)
- 45 mm tires: about 35 to 45 PSI (2.4 to 3.1 bar)
- 50 mm tires: about 30 to 40 PSI (2.1 to 2.8 bar)

Tubeless setups can run 3 to 5 PSI lower than tubed setups with the same tire, because the tubeless bead seats well and resists pinch flats better. Test your own setup. Start at the middle of the range, ride a loop, then adjust in steps of 2 to 3 PSI.

Signs the pressure is too high: the bike skips across loose gravel, the ride feels hard, and the tire loses traction in corners. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms or rolls off the rim in hard corners, and the rim bottoms out on rocks.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are typically 2.1 to 2.6 inches wide, and many are tubeless. Pressure is the main tool for traction, cornering, and avoiding pinch flats on rocks and roots. Mountain bikes run much lower pressure than road or gravel bikes.

A common starting point for a 75 kg (165 lb) rider:

- Cross country, 2.2 inch tires: about 22 to 28 PSI front and rear
- Trail, 2.3 to 2.4 inch tires: about 20 to 25 PSI front, 22 to 27 PSI rear
- Enduro or downhill, 2.4 to 2.6 inch tires: about 18 to 23 PSI front, 20 to 25 PSI rear

Run the rear tire slightly higher than the front. The rear carries less weight, so it can hold a slightly higher pressure without losing grip, and it helps keep the rear wheel from pinching.

Adjust for rider weight. Lighter riders can drop 2 to 3 PSI, and heavier riders may need 2 to 3 PSI more. Rough, rocky, or wet trails call for lower pressure. Dry, hardpacked, fast trails call for more.

Signs the pressure is too high: the bike feels skittish, the tire skips off corners and rocks, and the ride feels harsh. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms in turns, the rim hits rocks and dents or pinches, and the tire may burp air from the bead.

## Testing and adjusting

1. Set pressure with the tire cold.
2. Ride a short loop on the surface you usually ride.
3. Note how the tire handles corners, bumps, and braking.
4. Change pressure in small steps, 2 to 3 PSI at a time, until the tire grips and rides well without bottoming out.
5. Write down the final numbers for each wheel, tire model, and terrain, so you can set them again quickly.

## Safety

- Never exceed the maximum pressure on the sidewall. Overinflation can burst a tire or rim.
- Tubeless and tubed tires use different rim tape or valve rules. Follow the rim maker's guidance.
- Carry a spare tube or plug kit and a pump or CO2 inflator for trail and road rides.
- Inspect tires for cuts, bulges, and worn tread before each ride.

These figures are starting points. Your own weight, tire model, and riding style matter more than any table.

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, and the chance of a pinch flat. The right number depends on rider weight, tire width, tire casing, terrain, and whether the tire is tubed or tubeless. Always check the pressure range printed on the tire sidewall first. Never exceed the maximum.

## Basics that apply to all bikes

- Pressure is measured in PSI (pounds per square inch) or bar. 1 bar is about 14.5 PSI.
- Use a gauge. Pumps with built-in gauges can read 5 to 10 PSI off, so check with a separate gauge when accuracy matters.
- Check pressure cold, before riding. Tires lose about 1 to 2 PSI per week through the tube or tire, and warm tires read higher after a ride.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure than narrow tires at the same load. Pressure and width work together.
- Heavier riders, or riders carrying packs or panniers, need more pressure.
- Wet, slick, or loose surfaces call for lower pressure for more contact patch and grip.

## Road bikes

Road tires are narrow, usually 23 to 32 mm, and run at high pressure. The main goals are low rolling resistance and a smooth ride on paved surfaces.

A common starting point for a 70 kg (155 lb) rider:

- 23 mm tires: about 100 to 110 PSI (6.9 to 7.6 bar)
- 25 mm tires: about 90 to 100 PSI (6.2 to 6.9 bar)
- 28 mm tires: about 80 to 90 PSI (5.5 to 6.2 bar)
- 32 mm tires: about 65 to 80 PSI (4.5 to 5.5 bar)

Adjust by rider weight. Add about 5 PSI for each 10 kg above 70 kg, and subtract about 5 PSI for each 10 kg below it. Wider tires and rougher roads both justify dropping 5 to 10 PSI from these figures.

Signs the pressure is too high: a harsh, bouncy ride, rim strikes on bumps, and reduced grip in corners. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms in corners, feels soft on pedaling, or the rim contacts the road on hard hits. Pinch flats become more likely at low pressure on rough roads.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are typically 35 to 50 mm wide. Lower pressure gives grip on loose dirt, gravel, and mixed pavement, and it absorbs vibration on long rides.

A common starting point for a 70 kg (155 lb) rider:

- 35 mm tires: about 45 to 55 PSI (3.1 to 3.8 bar)
- 40 mm tires: about 40 to 50 PSI (2.8 to 3.4 bar)
- 45 mm tires: about 35 to 45 PSI (2.4 to 3.1 bar)
- 50 mm tires: about 30 to 40 PSI (2.1 to 2.8 bar)

Tubeless setups can run 3 to 5 PSI lower than tubed setups with the same tire, because the tubeless bead seats well and resists pinch flats better. Test your own setup. Start at the middle of the range, ride a loop, then adjust in steps of 2 to 3 PSI.

Signs the pressure is too high: the bike skips across loose gravel, the ride feels hard, and the tire loses traction in corners. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms or rolls off the rim in hard corners, and the rim bottoms out on rocks.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are typically 2.1 to 2.6 inches wide, and many are tubeless. Pressure is the main tool for traction, cornering, and avoiding pinch flats on rocks and roots. Mountain bikes run much lower pressure than road or gravel bikes.

A common starting point for a 75 kg (165 lb) rider:

- Cross country, 2.2 inch tires: about 22 to 28 PSI front and rear
- Trail, 2.3 to 2.4 inch tires: about 20 to 25 PSI front, 22 to 27 PSI rear
- Enduro or downhill, 2.4 to 2.6 inch tires: about 18 to 23 PSI front, 20 to 25 PSI rear

Run the rear tire slightly higher than the front. The rear carries less weight, so it can hold a slightly higher pressure without losing grip, and it helps keep the rear wheel from pinching.

Adjust for rider weight. Lighter riders can drop 2 to 3 PSI, and heavier riders may need 2 to 3 PSI more. Rough, rocky, or wet trails call for lower pressure. Dry, hardpacked, fast trails call for more.

Signs the pressure is too high: the bike feels skittish, the tire skips off corners and rocks, and the ride feels harsh. Signs it is too low: the tire squirms in turns, the rim hits rocks and dents or pinches, and the tire may burp air from the bead.

## Testing and adjusting

1. Set pressure with the tire cold.
2. Ride a short loop on the surface you usually ride.
3. Note how the tire handles corners, bumps, and braking.
4. Change pressure in small steps, 2 to 3 PSI at a time, until the tire grips and rides well without bottoming out.
5. Write down the final numbers for each wheel, tire model, and terrain, so you can set them again quickly.

## Safety

- Never exceed the maximum pressure on the sidewall. Overinflation can burst a tire or rim.
- Tubeless and tubed tires use different rim tape or valve rules. Follow the rim maker's guidance.
- Carry a spare tube or plug kit and a pump or CO2 inflator for trail and road rides.
- Inspect tires for cuts, bulges, and worn tread before each ride.

These figures are starting points. Your own weight, tire model, and riding style matter more than any table.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects rolling speed, grip, comfort, pinch flat risk and handling. The ranges below are starting points. Your rider weight, tire width, rim width and terrain decide the final number.

## Before you start

* Check the sidewall. Every tire prints a maximum and sometimes a minimum pressure. Never exceed the maximum.
* Measure with a gauge you trust. Gas station gauges and cheap dial gauges can read 5 psi or more off.
* Set pressure cold, before riding. Pressure rises as the tire warms and falls over days or weeks.
* Pressure is a range, not one correct number. Small changes of 2 to 3 psi are noticeable, so adjust in small steps.
* Rider weight includes gear you carry on the bike, such as a pack, bottles and tools.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide and run at high pressure. Higher pressure lowers rolling resistance on smooth pavement, up to the point where the tire starts to feel harsh and loses grip on rough surfaces.

**Typical ranges (tubed or tubeless, smooth pavement):**

* 23 mm: about 90 to 120 psi
* 25 mm: about 80 to 110 psi
* 28 mm: about 70 to 95 psi
* 32 mm: about 60 to 85 psi

Rider weight shifts these numbers. A heavier rider needs more pressure to keep the tire from squirming and to avoid pinch flats. A lighter rider can run lower. As a rough guide, a rider near 70 kg (155 lb) on 25 mm tires often runs around 85 to 95 psi, and a rider near 90 kg (200 lb) often runs around 95 to 105 psi.

**Factors that change the number:**

* Wider rims: a wide internal rim spreads the tire, so the same tire runs at lower pressure. Check the rim width and the tire fit chart.
* Road quality: rough chip seal or broken roads call for 5 to 10 psi less than smooth tarmac.
* Tubeless: tubeless setups often run 5 to 10 psi lower than tubes at the same width, because sealant protects against pinch flats.
* Wet weather: 3 to 5 psi less can improve grip on wet surfaces.

**Warning signs:**

* Pressure too high: harsh ride, skipping over bumps, loss of grip in corners, fatigue on long rides.
* Pressure too low: the tire squirms in corners, the rim may hit the ground over hard bumps, pinch flats increase, and the tire may roll off the rim.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. They run much lower than road tires because loose dirt, gravel, mud and washboard need the tire to conform to the ground.

**Typical ranges (tubeless recommended, mixed gravel):**

* 35 mm: about 35 to 45 psi
* 38 mm: about 32 to 42 psi
* 40 mm: about 30 to 40 psi
* 45 mm and wider: about 25 to 35 psi

These numbers assume a rider around 70 to 80 kg (155 to 175 lb). Heavier riders should add 2 to 5 psi. Lighter riders can drop 2 to 5 psi.

**Adjust for terrain:**

* Smooth gravel or fast roads: use the higher end of the range for speed and lower rolling resistance.
* Loose, sandy or washboard surfaces: use the lower end for traction and comfort.
* Rocky descents: a little lower can help the tire wrap around rocks, but drop too far and you risk pinch flats or a burp.
* Mud: lower pressure gives more grip. Go down in small steps and check the tire does not roll off the bead.

**Tubeless or tubes:** Tubeless gravel setups allow the lowest safe pressures because sealant plugs small punctures and the tire does not pinch against the rim. Tubes need a bit more pressure to avoid pinch flats at the same width.

**Warning signs:**

* Too high: bouncy, skittish handling, the bike skips over loose ground, and less grip in corners.
* Too low: the tire squirms, rolls off the bead, bottoms out on bumps, and pinch flats or rim damage become likely.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, often with knobby treads. Pressure is the main tool for grip and comfort on trails. Most riders run tubeless.

**Typical ranges (tubeless, trail riding, 75 to 85 kg rider):**

* 2.2 inch tire: front about 22 to 26 psi, rear about 24 to 28 psi
* 2.3 to 2.4 inch tire: front about 20 to 24 psi, rear about 22 to 26 psi
* 2.5 to 2.6 inch tire: front about 18 to 22 psi, rear about 20 to 24 psi

Run the rear 1 to 3 psi higher than the front. The rear carries more of the rider weight on most bikes.

**Adjust for rider weight and conditions:**

* Heavier riders add 2 to 4 psi. Lighter riders can subtract 2 to 4 psi.
* Rocky or rooty trails: a little lower improves grip and absorbs impacts, but stay above the minimum for your rim and tire to avoid burping or rim damage.
* Smooth, fast or dry trails: go a little higher for speed and less rolling resistance.
* Wet or loamy conditions: a little lower gives more traction on roots and wet rock.
* Enduro or downhill riding with aggressive descents: many riders run 2 to 4 psi lower than cross country setups.

**Tubeless and tubes:** Tubeless tires can run lower than tubed tires because the tire does not pinch the tube against the rim. If you run tubes, stay higher to avoid pinch flats and check the minimum pressure printed on the tire.

**Warning signs:**

* Too high: skating across rocks, loss of traction, harsh ride, and fatigue on long descents.
* Too low: the tire rolls off the bead, the rim dents or bends, the tire feels squishy in corners, and tubeless setups may burp air.

## Quick reference

| Bike type | Typical width | Typical pressure | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Road | 23 to 32 mm | 60 to 120 psi | Higher for narrow tires and lighter riders |
| Gravel | 35 to 50 mm | 25 to 45 psi | Lower for loose or rough terrain |
| Mountain | 2.2 to 2.6 in | 18 to 28 psi | Rear 1 to 3 psi higher than front |

## Testing your pressure

1. Start at the middle of the range for your tire and rider weight.
2. Ride a familiar loop. Note traction, comfort and any squirming.
3. Adjust by 2 to 3 psi at a time.
4. Check for pinch flats, tire roll off and rim dents after rough rides.
5. Recheck pressure after a few days, since tubes and tubeless tires lose some air over time.

These figures are general guidance. Always stay within the maximum and minimum pressures printed on your tire and the rim manufacturer's limits.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects rolling speed, grip, comfort, pinch flat risk and handling. The ranges below are starting points. Your rider weight, tire width, rim width and terrain decide the final number.

## Before you start

* Check the sidewall. Every tire prints a maximum and sometimes a minimum pressure. Never exceed the maximum.
* Measure with a gauge you trust. Gas station gauges and cheap dial gauges can read 5 psi or more off.
* Set pressure cold, before riding. Pressure rises as the tire warms and falls over days or weeks.
* Pressure is a range, not one correct number. Small changes of 2 to 3 psi are noticeable, so adjust in small steps.
* Rider weight includes gear you carry on the bike, such as a pack, bottles and tools.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide and run at high pressure. Higher pressure lowers rolling resistance on smooth pavement, up to the point where the tire starts to feel harsh and loses grip on rough surfaces.

**Typical ranges (tubed or tubeless, smooth pavement):**

* 23 mm: about 90 to 120 psi
* 25 mm: about 80 to 110 psi
* 28 mm: about 70 to 95 psi
* 32 mm: about 60 to 85 psi

Rider weight shifts these numbers. A heavier rider needs more pressure to keep the tire from squirming and to avoid pinch flats. A lighter rider can run lower. As a rough guide, a rider near 70 kg (155 lb) on 25 mm tires often runs around 85 to 95 psi, and a rider near 90 kg (200 lb) often runs around 95 to 105 psi.

**Factors that change the number:**

* Wider rims: a wide internal rim spreads the tire, so the same tire runs at lower pressure. Check the rim width and the tire fit chart.
* Road quality: rough chip seal or broken roads call for 5 to 10 psi less than smooth tarmac.
* Tubeless: tubeless setups often run 5 to 10 psi lower than tubes at the same width, because sealant protects against pinch flats.
* Wet weather: 3 to 5 psi less can improve grip on wet surfaces.

**Warning signs:**

* Pressure too high: harsh ride, skipping over bumps, loss of grip in corners, fatigue on long rides.
* Pressure too low: the tire squirms in corners, the rim may hit the ground over hard bumps, pinch flats increase, and the tire may roll off the rim.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. They run much lower than road tires because loose dirt, gravel, mud and washboard need the tire to conform to the ground.

**Typical ranges (tubeless recommended, mixed gravel):**

* 35 mm: about 35 to 45 psi
* 38 mm: about 32 to 42 psi
* 40 mm: about 30 to 40 psi
* 45 mm and wider: about 25 to 35 psi

These numbers assume a rider around 70 to 80 kg (155 to 175 lb). Heavier riders should add 2 to 5 psi. Lighter riders can drop 2 to 5 psi.

**Adjust for terrain:**

* Smooth gravel or fast roads: use the higher end of the range for speed and lower rolling resistance.
* Loose, sandy or washboard surfaces: use the lower end for traction and comfort.
* Rocky descents: a little lower can help the tire wrap around rocks, but drop too far and you risk pinch flats or a burp.
* Mud: lower pressure gives more grip. Go down in small steps and check the tire does not roll off the bead.

**Tubeless or tubes:** Tubeless gravel setups allow the lowest safe pressures because sealant plugs small punctures and the tire does not pinch against the rim. Tubes need a bit more pressure to avoid pinch flats at the same width.

**Warning signs:**

* Too high: bouncy, skittish handling, the bike skips over loose ground, and less grip in corners.
* Too low: the tire squirms, rolls off the bead, bottoms out on bumps, and pinch flats or rim damage become likely.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, often with knobby treads. Pressure is the main tool for grip and comfort on trails. Most riders run tubeless.

**Typical ranges (tubeless, trail riding, 75 to 85 kg rider):**

* 2.2 inch tire: front about 22 to 26 psi, rear about 24 to 28 psi
* 2.3 to 2.4 inch tire: front about 20 to 24 psi, rear about 22 to 26 psi
* 2.5 to 2.6 inch tire: front about 18 to 22 psi, rear about 20 to 24 psi

Run the rear 1 to 3 psi higher than the front. The rear carries more of the rider weight on most bikes.

**Adjust for rider weight and conditions:**

* Heavier riders add 2 to 4 psi. Lighter riders can subtract 2 to 4 psi.
* Rocky or rooty trails: a little lower improves grip and absorbs impacts, but stay above the minimum for your rim and tire to avoid burping or rim damage.
* Smooth, fast or dry trails: go a little higher for speed and less rolling resistance.
* Wet or loamy conditions: a little lower gives more traction on roots and wet rock.
* Enduro or downhill riding with aggressive descents: many riders run 2 to 4 psi lower than cross country setups.

**Tubeless and tubes:** Tubeless tires can run lower than tubed tires because the tire does not pinch the tube against the rim. If you run tubes, stay higher to avoid pinch flats and check the minimum pressure printed on the tire.

**Warning signs:**

* Too high: skating across rocks, loss of traction, harsh ride, and fatigue on long descents.
* Too low: the tire rolls off the bead, the rim dents or bends, the tire feels squishy in corners, and tubeless setups may burp air.

## Quick reference

| Bike type | Typical width | Typical pressure | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Road | 23 to 32 mm | 60 to 120 psi | Higher for narrow tires and lighter riders |
| Gravel | 35 to 50 mm | 25 to 45 psi | Lower for loose or rough terrain |
| Mountain | 2.2 to 2.6 in | 18 to 28 psi | Rear 1 to 3 psi higher than front |

## Testing your pressure

1. Start at the middle of the range for your tire and rider weight.
2. Ride a familiar loop. Note traction, comfort and any squirming.
3. Adjust by 2 to 3 psi at a time.
4. Check for pinch flats, tire roll off and rim dents after rough rides.
5. Recheck pressure after a few days, since tubes and tubeless tires lose some air over time.

These figures are general guidance. Always stay within the maximum and minimum pressures printed on your tire and the rim manufacturer's limits.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

These figures are starting points for an adult rider of about 70 to 80 kg (155 to 175 lb) on a bike with a typical load. Always stay below the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Adjust in small steps of 1 to 2 psi (0.1 to 0.15 bar) and note what feels best on your routes.

## How pressure works

Pressure controls how much the tire deforms over bumps. Lower pressure gives more grip and comfort and reduces the chance of pinch flats. Higher pressure lowers rolling resistance on smooth surfaces but transmits more shock and gives less grip. Four factors shape the right number:

* Rider and load weight. Heavier loads need more pressure to keep the same tire shape.
* Tire width. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same feel.
* Rim width. A wider rim supports a wider tire at the same pressure and gives a larger, more stable contact patch. Check the rim width recommendation for your tire size.
* Surface and conditions. Wet, loose or rough ground calls for lower pressure. Smooth, dry pavement calls for higher pressure.

Tubeless tires can run about 5 to 10 psi lower than tubed tires with the same width, because the sealant and the absence of an inner tube reduce the risk of a pinch flat.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Most riders run them between 60 and 110 psi.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider on smooth pavement:

* 23 mm: 90 to 110 psi (6.2 to 7.6 bar)
* 25 mm: 80 to 100 psi (5.5 to 6.9 bar)
* 28 mm: 70 to 90 psi (4.8 to 6.2 bar)
* 32 mm: 60 to 80 psi (4.1 to 5.5 bar)

Adjustments:

* Lighter riders (under 60 kg) can often drop 5 to 10 psi from the low end of the range.
* Heavier riders (over 90 kg) should stay near the top of the range or go a little higher.
* Wet roads, cobbles, or rough chip-seal call for 5 to 10 psi less than dry, smooth tarmac.
* Race days on smooth roads may favour the upper end for the lowest rolling resistance.

Typical mistake: riders inflate road tires to the sidewall maximum by default. A tire at 120 psi on rough roads often feels harsh and can lose grip on wet corners.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Lower pressure gives grip on loose surfaces, and tires with a larger volume absorb washboard and rocks.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider:

* 35 mm: 35 to 45 psi (2.4 to 3.1 bar)
* 38 to 40 mm: 32 to 40 psi (2.2 to 2.8 bar)
* 43 to 45 mm: 28 to 36 psi (1.9 to 2.5 bar)
* 50 mm: 25 to 32 psi (1.7 to 2.2 bar)

Adjustments:

* Tubeless setups can run 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed setups with the same tire.
* Loose gravel, sand, and climbs favour the low end of the range for traction.
* Fast, hard-packed roads favour the high end for less rolling resistance.
* Bikepacking with heavy bags: add 2 to 4 psi to the rear tire.

A practical check: when you press the tire sidewall with your thumb, it should give a little but not feel soft or squirm in corners. If the rim touches the ground on hits, the pressure is too low.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.0 to 2.6 inches wide, and most run tubeless. Mountain bike pressures are low, and the front tire often runs a few psi lower than the rear because it carries more weight during braking and steering.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider on a 30 mm internal-width rim, tubeless:

* Cross-country, 2.2 to 2.4 inch: 22 to 28 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar) front, 24 to 30 psi (1.7 to 2.1 bar) rear
* Trail, 2.4 to 2.5 inch: 20 to 26 psi (1.4 to 1.8 bar) front, 22 to 28 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar) rear
* Enduro and downhill, 2.5 to 2.6 inch: 18 to 24 psi (1.2 to 1.7 bar) front, 20 to 26 psi (1.4 to 1.8 bar) rear

Adjustments:

* Heavier riders should add 2 to 4 psi. Lighter riders should subtract 2 to 4 psi.
* Wet, muddy, or loose terrain calls for the low end of the range.
* Hardpack, fast flow trails, or rocky descents with a lot of impact may call for a slight increase.
* Tire inserts such as foam or tubes change the feel. Start about 2 psi higher with an insert and test from there.
* Wider rims support lower pressures. Narrow rims let the tire roll over and pinch more easily.

If you feel the rim strike rock or root hits, add 1 to 2 psi. If the tire feels bouncy, squirmy or rolls over sidewalls in corners, reduce pressure in small steps.

## Measuring and setting pressure

* Use a dedicated pressure gauge. Floor pumps often have built-in gauges, but a separate gauge helps you compare readings.
* Check pressure with cold tires, before riding or after the bike has sat for a while. Riding warms the tire and raises pressure slightly.
* Temperature changes pressure. Roughly, pressure drops about 1 psi for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit (about 5 degrees Celsius) of cooling. A tire set on a warm afternoon may read low on a cold morning.
* Tires lose air over time. Road tires can lose several psi a week, and tubeless tires lose air through the tire and sealant. Check before every ride.
* Presta valves need the small locking nut loosened before inflating and tightened afterward. Schrader valves work with standard car-style chucks.
* Never exceed the maximum pressure on the tire sidewall or the rim's maximum pressure marking. Inflate slowly and stop when you reach your target.

## Quick reference

* Road 25 mm, 75 kg rider, dry pavement: about 90 psi front and 95 psi rear.
* Gravel 40 mm, tubeless, 75 kg rider: about 34 psi front and 36 psi rear.
* Mountain 2.4 inch trail, tubeless, 75 kg rider: about 22 psi front and 25 psi rear.

These numbers are starting points. Riders and tire models differ, so tune from there.

* Rider and load weight. Heavier loads need more pressure to keep the same tire shape.
* Tire width. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same feel.
* Rim width. A wider rim supports a wider tire at the same pressure and gives a larger, more stable contact patch. Check the rim width recommendation for your tire size.
* Surface and conditions. Wet, loose or rough ground calls for lower pressure. Smooth, dry pavement calls for higher pressure.

Tubeless tires can run about 5 to 10 psi lower than tubed tires with the same width, because the sealant and the absence of an inner tube reduce the risk of a pinch flat.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Most riders run them between 60 and 110 psi.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider on smooth pavement:

* 23 mm: 90 to 110 psi (6.2 to 7.6 bar)
* 25 mm: 80 to 100 psi (5.5 to 6.9 bar)
* 28 mm: 70 to 90 psi (4.8 to 6.2 bar)
* 32 mm: 60 to 80 psi (4.1 to 5.5 bar)

Adjustments:

* Lighter riders (under 60 kg) can often drop 5 to 10 psi from the low end of the range.
* Heavier riders (over 90 kg) should stay near the top of the range or go a little higher.
* Wet roads, cobbles, or rough chip-seal call for 5 to 10 psi less than dry, smooth tarmac.
* Race days on smooth roads may favour the upper end for the lowest rolling resistance.

Typical mistake: riders inflate road tires to the sidewall maximum by default. A tire at 120 psi on rough roads often feels harsh and can lose grip on wet corners.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Lower pressure gives grip on loose surfaces, and tires with a larger volume absorb washboard and rocks.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider:

* 35 mm: 35 to 45 psi (2.4 to 3.1 bar)
* 38 to 40 mm: 32 to 40 psi (2.2 to 2.8 bar)
* 43 to 45 mm: 28 to 36 psi (1.9 to 2.5 bar)
* 50 mm: 25 to 32 psi (1.7 to 2.2 bar)

Adjustments:

* Tubeless setups can run 3 to 5 psi lower than tubed setups with the same tire.
* Loose gravel, sand, and climbs favour the low end of the range for traction.
* Fast, hard-packed roads favour the high end for less rolling resistance.
* Bikepacking with heavy bags: add 2 to 4 psi to the rear tire.

A practical check: when you press the tire sidewall with your thumb, it should give a little but not feel soft or squirm in corners. If the rim touches the ground on hits, the pressure is too low.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.0 to 2.6 inches wide, and most run tubeless. Mountain bike pressures are low, and the front tire often runs a few psi lower than the rear because it carries more weight during braking and steering.

Approximate starting ranges for a 70 to 80 kg rider on a 30 mm internal-width rim, tubeless:

* Cross-country, 2.2 to 2.4 inch: 22 to 28 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar) front, 24 to 30 psi (1.7 to 2.1 bar) rear
* Trail, 2.4 to 2.5 inch: 20 to 26 psi (1.4 to 1.8 bar) front, 22 to 28 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar) rear
* Enduro and downhill, 2.5 to 2.6 inch: 18 to 24 psi (1.2 to 1.7 bar) front, 20 to 26 psi (1.4 to 1.8 bar) rear

Adjustments:

* Heavier riders should add 2 to 4 psi. Lighter riders should subtract 2 to 4 psi.
* Wet, muddy, or loose terrain calls for the low end of the range.
* Hardpack, fast flow trails, or rocky descents with a lot of impact may call for a slight increase.
* Tire inserts such as foam or tubes change the feel. Start about 2 psi higher with an insert and test from there.
* Wider rims support lower pressures. Narrow rims let the tire roll over and pinch more easily.

If you feel the rim strike rock or root hits, add 1 to 2 psi. If the tire feels bouncy, squirmy or rolls over sidewalls in corners, reduce pressure in small steps.

## Measuring and setting pressure

* Use a dedicated pressure gauge. Floor pumps often have built-in gauges, but a separate gauge helps you compare readings.
* Check pressure with cold tires, before riding or after the bike has sat for a while. Riding warms the tire and raises pressure slightly.
* Temperature changes pressure. Roughly, pressure drops about 1 psi for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit (about 5 degrees Celsius) of cooling. A tire set on a warm afternoon may read low on a cold morning.
* Tires lose air over time. Road tires can lose several psi a week, and tubeless tires lose air through the tire and sealant. Check before every ride.
* Presta valves need the small locking nut loosened before inflating and tightened afterward. Schrader valves work with standard car-style chucks.
* Never exceed the maximum pressure on the tire sidewall or the rim's maximum pressure marking. Inflate slowly and stop when you reach your target.

## Quick reference

* Road 25 mm, 75 kg rider, dry pavement: about 90 psi front and 95 psi rear.
* Gravel 40 mm, tubeless, 75 kg rider: about 34 psi front and 36 psi rear.
* Mountain 2.4 inch trail, tubeless, 75 kg rider: about 22 psi front and 25 psi rear.

These numbers are starting points. Riders and tire models differ, so tune from there.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

These ranges are starting points. Always check the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall and never exceed it.

## Why pressure matters

Pressure controls three things: rolling resistance, grip, and pinch flat risk. Too little pressure makes the tire squirm, wastes energy and can pinch the tube on bumps. Too much pressure makes the bike bounce, reduces grip on loose or wet surfaces and feels harsh.

## Measuring and checking

* Use a gauge you trust. Floor pumps with built-in gauges can be off by several psi.
* Check pressure before every ride, when the tires are cold.
* Pressure rises when the air warms up. A tire inflated in a cold garage will read higher on a sunny road.
* Tubeless tires lose air through the casing over days, so top them up before rides.

## Road bikes

Typical tire widths are 23 to 28 mm. Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same comfort and grip.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 70 kg (155 lb) on a rim of typical modern internal width:

* 23 mm: about 90 to 100 psi (6.2 to 6.9 bar)
* 25 mm: about 85 to 95 psi (5.9 to 6.5 bar)
* 28 mm: about 75 to 85 psi (5.2 to 5.9 bar)

Adjustments:

* Heavier riders need more pressure. Lighter riders need less.
* Wet roads or rough chip seal: drop 5 to 10 psi for more grip and comfort.
* Smooth, dry, race conditions: the upper end of the range.
* Wide rims: a wider rim spreads the tire, so run a little lower than the same tire on a narrow rim.
* Tubeless: many riders run 5 to 10 psi lower than tubed tires at the same width.

## Gravel bikes

Typical tire widths are 35 to 50 mm. Gravel riding mixes pavement, dirt and loose surfaces, so the pressure is much lower than on road tires.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 75 kg (165 lb), tubeless:

* 35 mm: about 35 to 42 psi (2.4 to 2.9 bar)
* 40 mm: about 32 to 38 psi (2.2 to 2.6 bar)
* 45 to 50 mm: about 28 to 34 psi (1.9 to 2.3 bar)

Adjustments:

* Loose gravel or sand: go lower, toward the bottom of the range, for more traction.
* Hard pack or pavement-heavy routes: go higher, toward the top, for speed and fewer pinch flats.
* Tubed tires need about 3 to 6 psi more than tubeless to avoid pinch flats.
* Heavier loads such as bikepacking bags: add 2 to 4 psi.

## Mountain bikes

Typical tire widths are 2.2 to 2.6 inches for trail bikes and 2.5 to 2.8 inches for enduro and downhill bikes. Mountain tires are run low because the suspension and the tire volume absorb the impacts.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 75 kg (165 lb), tubeless, on a rim of about 30 mm internal width:

* Cross-country, 2.2 inch: about 24 to 28 psi (1.7 to 1.9 bar) front and rear
* Trail, 2.4 inch: about 22 to 26 psi (1.5 to 1.8 bar)
* Enduro or downhill, 2.5 to 2.6 inch: about 20 to 24 psi (1.4 to 1.7 bar)

Adjustments:

* Run the front 1 to 2 psi lower than the rear. The front carries more weight under braking and steering.
* Rough, rocky, or high-speed terrain: go up 1 to 2 psi to avoid rim strikes.
* Loose, dry, or root-heavy terrain: go down 1 to 2 psi for more grip.
* Wider rims: lower the pressure slightly, because a wider rim gives the tire a bigger footprint.
* Lighter riders: start at the bottom of the range. Heavier riders: start at the top.

Signs the pressure is too low: the tire rolls off the rim in corners, the rim makes a dent in the tire sidewall, or you hear a hiss or thud on the rim strike. Signs it is too high: the bike skips over small bumps, the tire slides on turns, and the ride feels harsh.

## Quick reference

| Discipline | Typical width | Typical pressure range |
|---|---|---|
| Road | 23 to 28 mm | 75 to 100 psi |
| Gravel | 35 to 50 mm | 28 to 42 psi (tubeless) |
| Mountain | 2.2 to 2.8 in | 20 to 28 psi (tubeless) |

The final pressure is a matter of feel. Start in the middle of the range, ride a short loop, and adjust by 1 to 2 psi at a time.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, pinch flat risk, and handling. The right pressure depends on your weight, the tire width, the surface, and your riding style. Use the ranges below as starting points, then adjust by feel.

## Why pressure matters

- **Too high:** less grip, a harsh ride, and more vibration. Narrow, hard tires can skip on wet or loose surfaces.
- **Too low:** more rolling resistance, sluggish handling, and a higher risk of pinch flats (the tube or tire is pinched against the rim on an impact) and rim damage. Tubeless tires can also burp air or roll off the rim.
- **Right:** the tire deforms slightly over bumps, keeps contact with the ground, and rolls efficiently.

## Factors that change your number

- **Rider and load weight.** Heavier riders need more pressure. Add a few psi when carrying a heavy pack or panniers.
- **Tire width.** Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same feel. A 28 mm tire and a 32 mm tire at the same pressure will ride differently.
- **Surface.** Smooth pavement favors higher pressure. Rough, wet, or loose ground favors lower pressure.
- **Tubed or tubeless.** Tubeless tires can run 3 to 8 psi lower than tubed tires with the same width, because the sealant and bead design resist pinch flats better.
- **Rim width.** Wider internal rim widths support a wider tire at a given pressure and change the tire profile. Check the rim and tire manufacturer's pressure chart when they differ.
- **Manufacturer limits.** Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the sidewall.

## Road bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 23 to 28 mm.
**Typical pressure:** about 80 to 120 psi for a 25 mm tire, depending on rider weight.

How to start:

- Rider weight under 130 lb (59 kg): about 80 to 95 psi.
- Rider weight 130 to 170 lb (59 to 77 kg): about 95 to 110 psi.
- Rider weight over 170 lb (77 kg): about 105 to 120 psi.
- For 28 mm or wider road tires, drop about 5 to 10 psi from these numbers.
- Wet roads or rough chip seal: drop 5 to 10 psi for more grip and comfort.

Road riders often run higher pressure than they expect. Many modern tires ride well and roll fast at lower pressure, so test a few settings on your usual route.

## Gravel bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 35 to 50 mm.
**Typical pressure:** about 30 to 50 psi, depending on width, weight, and surface.

How to start:

- Smooth gravel or mixed pavement: 40 to 50 psi.
- Loose or fast gravel: 30 to 40 psi.
- Rough, washboard, or technical gravel: 25 to 35 psi on tubeless setups.
- Heavier riders and wider tires: move toward the upper end of the range.
- Tubed setups: stay at the higher end of each range to avoid pinch flats.

Tip: a common approach is to start at the middle of the range, ride a loop, and adjust 2 to 3 psi at a time. Note what feels fast, what feels secure in corners, and what feels harsh.

## Mountain bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 2.2 to 2.6 inches (about 56 to 66 mm), with wider options for enduro and downhill.
**Typical pressure:** about 18 to 30 psi, depending on weight, width, and terrain.

How to start:

- Rider weight under 150 lb (68 kg): about 20 to 24 psi.
- Rider weight 150 to 190 lb (68 to 86 kg): about 22 to 26 psi.
- Rider weight over 190 lb (86 kg): about 24 to 30 psi.
- Tubeless setups: go 2 to 4 psi lower than the figures above for more traction and less harshness.
- Tubed setups: stay at the higher end to avoid pinch flats.
- Hardpacked trail and dry conditions: run slightly higher.
- Wet roots, loose rock, or steep descents: run lower for grip, but avoid bottoming out the rim.

For aggressive trail or downhill riding, many riders run lower pressure front and rear, with the rear slightly higher for pedaling efficiency. Experiment in small steps.

## Measuring and checking

- Use a quality gauge. Dial and digital gauges on pumps are often inaccurate, so check against a separate gauge.
- Check pressure before every ride. Tires lose pressure over time, and tubeless tires can lose pressure faster.
- Measure when the tires are cold, since heat from riding and sun raises pressure.
- Use a tire pressure chart from your tire or rim maker when available.

## Quick reference

| Bike type | Typical width | Typical pressure | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Road | 23 to 28 mm | 80 to 120 psi | Higher for lighter riders and smooth roads |
| Gravel | 35 to 50 mm | 30 to 50 psi | Lower for loose or rough ground |
| Mountain | 2.2 to 2.6 in | 18 to 30 psi | Tubeless runs lower than tubed |

These values are starting points. Adjust them by feel, and stay within the sidewall maximum.
