# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, pinch flat risk and handling. The right pressure depends on rider weight, tire width, terrain and tubeless or tube setup. Use the ranges below as starting points, then adjust by feel.

## Basics That Apply to Every Bike

- Pressure is measured in PSI (pounds per square inch) or bar. 1 bar is about 14.5 PSI.
- Heavier riders need more pressure. Light riders can run less.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure than narrow tires for the same grip and comfort.
- Tubeless tires can run a little lower than tubed tires without pinch flats, because there is no tube to pinch.
- Always stay within the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.
- Check pressure before every ride. Tires lose air over time, especially latex tubes.
- Use a gauge. Pumps without gauges give guesses.

## Road Bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 23 mm to 28 mm.

**Typical pressure:** 80 to 110 PSI (5.5 to 7.5 bar) for most riders.

**Rough guide by rider weight (tubed, 25 mm tire):**

| Rider weight | Starting pressure |
|---|---|
| Under 120 lb (55 kg) | 80 to 90 PSI |
| 120 to 150 lb (55 to 68 kg) | 90 to 100 PSI |
| 150 to 180 lb (68 to 82 kg) | 95 to 105 PSI |
| 180 to 200 lb (82 to 91 kg) | 100 to 110 PSI |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 105 to 115 PSI, check the sidewall maximum |

**Notes:**

- Wider tires (28 mm and up) run well at 75 to 95 PSI.
- Wet roads favor the lower end of the range for more grip.
- Dry, smooth pavement and fast group rides can use the higher end for lower rolling resistance.
- Going too high gives a harsh ride and less grip on rough pavement.

## Gravel Bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 35 mm to 50 mm.

**Typical pressure:** 25 to 45 PSI (1.7 to 3.1 bar) for most riders on tubeless setups. Tubed setups usually need 5 to 10 PSI more.

**Rough guide by rider weight (tubeless, 40 mm tire):**

| Rider weight | Smooth gravel | Rough or loose gravel |
|---|---|---|
| Under 130 lb (59 kg) | 30 to 35 PSI | 25 to 30 PSI |
| 130 to 170 lb (59 to 77 kg) | 33 to 38 PSI | 28 to 33 PSI |
| 170 to 200 lb (77 to 91 kg) | 36 to 42 PSI | 30 to 36 PSI |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 40 to 45 PSI | 34 to 40 PSI |

**Notes:**

- Lower pressure gives more grip, comfort and control on loose surfaces.
- Too low causes squirming in corners, rim strikes on bumps and burps (air loss through the bead) in tubeless setups.
- Wider tires run lower. A 50 mm tire may run 5 PSI lower than a 40 mm tire at the same weight.
- Heavy loads, such as bikepacking bags, call for a little more pressure.

## Mountain Bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 2.2 to 2.6 inches for trail bikes. Wider enduro and downhill tires run lower.

**Typical pressure:** 18 to 30 PSI (1.2 to 2.1 bar) for most riders on tubeless setups.

**Rough guide by rider weight (tubeless, 2.4 inch tire, trail riding):**

| Rider weight | Starting pressure |
|---|---|
| Under 130 lb (59 kg) | 20 to 23 PSI |
| 130 to 170 lb (59 to 77 kg) | 22 to 26 PSI |
| 170 to 200 lb (77 to 91 kg) | 24 to 28 PSI |
| Over 200 lb (91 kg) | 26 to 30 PSI |

**Adjustments:**

- Rear tire often runs 1 to 3 PSI higher than the front when the bike has more weight on the back.
- Rocky, rooty or technical trails: go a little lower for grip and bump absorption.
- Hardpack or fast, smooth trails: go a little higher for speed and less rolling resistance.
- Enduro and downhill riders often run 20 PSI or lower, with inserts or tubeless sealant to prevent rim damage.
- Tubed tires need 3 to 6 PSI more than tubeless to avoid pinch flats.

## How to Fine-Tune by Feel

1. Set the pressure from the table for your weight and tire.
2. Ride a short loop on your usual terrain.
3. If the tire feels harsh, squirmy, or the rim hits on bumps, adjust by 1 to 2 PSI and recheck.
4. If the tire rolls slowly, slides on corners, or you get pinch flats, adjust in the other direction.
5. Write down what works for each tire and terrain combination.

## Safety Notes

- Never exceed the sidewall maximum pressure.
- Inflate slowly and check the gauge. Tire beads can pop off the rim at high pressure if inflated quickly.
- Recheck pressure after mounting new tires and after the first few rides, because new tubeless setups can settle.
- Check that the rim and tire are compatible for the pressure you plan to run, especially with carbon rims.

## Summary

- Road: 80 to 110 PSI on 23 to 28 mm tires.
- Gravel: 25 to 45 PSI on 35 to 50 mm tires, tubeless preferred.
- Mountain: 18 to 30 PSI on 2.2 to 2.6 inch tires, tubeless preferred.

These figures are general starting points. Adjust for rider weight, tire model, rim width and personal preference.

# Tire Pressure Guide

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, pinch flat risk, and handling. The right pressure depends on rider weight, tire width, surface, and tire construction. Always stay within the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall.

## Starting Points

- Measure with a gauge you trust. Gas station gauges often read off by several PSI.
- Check pressure cold, before riding.
- Heavier riders need more pressure. Lighter riders can run less.
- Wider tires run at lower pressure than narrow tires for the same load.
- Tubeless tires can run roughly 5 to 10 percent lower than tubed tires at the same width, because sealant and the bead fit reduce pinch flat risk.
- Adjust in small steps, about 2 to 3 PSI at a time, and ride a loop to compare.

## Road Bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Typical pressures are 80 to 110 PSI for a 23 mm tire, 70 to 100 PSI for a 25 mm tire, and 60 to 90 PSI for a 28 mm tire, for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb). Heavier riders should add pressure, and lighter riders should subtract it.

- Higher pressure lowers rolling resistance on smooth pavement.
- Going too high makes the ride harsh and reduces grip on rough or wet roads.
- If you feel every crack in the road, drop 5 PSI and check again.
- Tubular and very narrow racing tires may run at the upper end of the range.
- Wet or cold conditions favor the lower end of the range for grip.

## Gravel Bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Typical pressures are 40 to 55 PSI for tubed tires and 30 to 45 PSI for tubeless tires, for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb). Surface changes the choice more than anything else.

- Loose gravel or sand: run lower, around 30 to 40 PSI, for traction and to keep the tire from washing out.
- Hard packed gravel or mixed roads: run in the middle, around 40 to 50 PSI.
- Pavement sections: run a little higher to reduce rolling resistance.
- Lower pressure absorbs chatter and reduces the chance of pinch flats on rocky trails.
- Test by pressing the tire sidewall with your thumb. If the tread deforms a lot and the rim feels close to the ground, go up a little.
- Heavier loads, such as bikepacking bags, need slightly more pressure.

## Mountain Bikes

Mountain bike tires are usually 2.1 to 2.6 inches wide. Typical pressures are 22 to 30 PSI for cross country tires, 20 to 27 PSI for trail tires, and 18 to 24 PSI for enduro and downhill tires, for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb). Tubeless setups run at the low end of these ranges.

- Lower pressure gives more grip, more traction on roots and rock, and more comfort.
- Too low causes burping, where the tire folds off the rim, and rim damage on hard hits.
- Front tires usually run 2 to 3 PSI lower than rear tires, because the front carries less weight and steers under braking.
- Use a bit more pressure for hardpack and fast trails, and less for loose, wet, or rooty trails.
- Heavy riders, or riders on e-bikes, should add a few PSI.
- Check pressure before each ride, because tubeless tires lose air slowly through the tread and sealant.

## Quick Reference

| Bike type | Typical width | Typical pressure (tubed) | Typical pressure (tubeless) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Road | 23 to 32 mm | 60 to 110 PSI | Not common |
| Gravel | 35 to 50 mm | 40 to 55 PSI | 30 to 45 PSI |
| Mountain | 2.1 to 2.6 in | 24 to 30 PSI | 20 to 27 PSI |

These values are starting points for a rider around 70 kg (155 lb). Adjust by feel, and never exceed the sidewall maximum.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, and pinch flat risk. The right number depends on rider weight, tire width, tire construction (tubed or tubeless), and terrain. Treat every number below as a starting point, then adjust by feel.

## Ground rules for any bike

- Never exceed the maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Check the rim maximum too, if it is stated.
- Measure pressure with a gauge when the tire is cold. Pumps and built-in gauges can be off by several psi.
- Pressure rises a little when the tire warms up on a ride, and drops with temperature. Check before each ride.
- Heavier riders, heavier loads, and wider tires need less pressure for the same feel and grip.
- Wider rims give a wider tire footprint, so pressure for a given tire width is often a bit lower on a wide rim.
- Tubeless tires can run lower pressure than tubed tires because a sealed tubeless system resists pinch flats, and the tire does not need to be as firm to stay on the rim.

## Road bikes

### Typical tire widths

Most road tires are 25 mm to 32 mm wide. Narrow tires (23 mm) are common on older or race bikes. Wider road tires are now common because they roll well at lower pressure and grip better on rough pavement.

### Starting pressures (tubed, rider about 70 kg or 155 lb)

| Tire width | Typical pressure |
|---|---|
| 23 mm | 100 to 115 psi |
| 25 mm | 90 to 105 psi |
| 28 mm | 80 to 95 psi |
| 32 mm | 70 to 85 psi |

### Adjusting

- Heavier rider: add about 5 psi for every 10 kg above 70 kg.
- Lighter rider: subtract about 5 psi for every 10 kg below 70 kg.
- Wet or rough roads: drop 5 to 10 psi for more grip and comfort, as long as you do not feel the rim hitting the ground on bumps.
- Smooth dry roads and racing: the upper end of the range gives the lowest rolling resistance on a smooth surface.

### Notes

- Pinch flats happen at low pressure over sharp bumps. Stay above the lower end of the range for tubed tires.
- Tubeless road setups often run 5 to 10 psi lower than the table for the same width.

## Gravel bikes

### Typical tire widths

Gravel tires usually run 35 mm to 50 mm wide. Gravel bikes take wide tires because the riding surface changes from smooth pavement to loose dirt, sand, and rocks.

### Starting pressures (tubeless, rider about 70 kg or 155 lb)

| Tire width | Typical pressure |
|---|---|
| 35 mm | 35 to 42 psi |
| 38 mm | 33 to 40 psi |
| 40 mm | 30 to 38 psi |
| 45 mm | 27 to 34 psi |
| 50 mm | 24 to 30 psi |

For tubed gravel tires, add about 5 psi to these figures.

### Adjusting

- Loose gravel, sand, or wet corners: go to the low end of the range or a little below, for more traction.
- Smooth hardpack or fast gravel roads: go to the upper end for less rolling resistance.
- Heavier rider or heavy bags: go to the upper end of the range.
- Lighter rider: go to the lower end.

### Notes

- Gravel riding is where tire pressure matters most. A change of 3 to 5 psi can change how the bike handles on loose corners.
- Tubeless is strongly recommended for gravel because it lets you run low pressure without pinch flats.
- Check that the tire bead is seated and sealed after you change pressure.

## Mountain bikes

### Typical tire widths

Mountain bike tires come in several sizes. Common widths are 2.2 to 2.6 inches for trail and cross country riding, and 2.6 to 2.8 inches (plus sizes) for enduro and downhill bikes. Wider and taller tires need lower pressure.

### Starting pressures (tubeless, rider about 75 kg or 165 lb)

| Tire width | Riding style | Typical pressure |
|---|---|---|
| 2.2 in to 2.3 in | Cross country, hardpack | 26 to 30 psi |
| 2.3 in to 2.4 in | Trail | 23 to 27 psi |
| 2.5 in to 2.6 in | Trail and all mountain | 21 to 25 psi |
| 2.6 in to 2.8 in plus | Enduro and downhill | 15 to 22 psi |

For tubed mountain bike tires, add about 3 to 5 psi to these figures.

### Adjusting

- Loose, dry, or fast terrain: start at the middle of the range and adjust down for grip.
- Wet roots, rock gardens, or steep descents: lower the pressure to gain grip and absorb hits. Stop lowering when the tire feels squirmy in corners or the rim starts to bottom out.
- Smooth climbs and racing: higher pressure reduces rolling resistance.
- Heavier rider or bike with luggage: add about 2 to 4 psi.
- Lighter rider: subtract about 2 to 3 psi.

### Notes

- Rim strikes and pinch flats are the main risk at low pressure. Tubeless with sealant reduces both.
- Check pressure after the first few rides on a new tire. Tubeless tires can lose air as the bead settles.
- Wider rims suit lower pressures and bigger tires. Narrow rims with wide tires can make the tire profile too round and reduce grip.

## Quick checks

- Road: the tire should show a slight bulge and not feel hard on bumps.
- Gravel: the tire should not roll or squirm in corners, and the ride should feel smooth on small bumps.
- Mountain: the tire should keep its shape in corners, and you should not hear rim strikes on big hits.

These figures are general guidance from common setup practice. Tire makers publish their own pressure ranges, and those ranges override this guide.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort and pinch flat risk. The numbers below are starting points. Adjust them to your weight, terrain and tire model, and always stay within the pressure range printed on the tire sidewall.

## Why pressure matters

Lower pressure gives the tire more contact with the ground, which raises grip and comfort but adds rolling resistance when the tire flexes too much. Higher pressure rolls faster on smooth surfaces but skips over bumps and loses grip. The best pressure is the lowest one that does not cause pinch flats, rim strikes or squirming in corners.

Two factors set the starting point:

* Rider and bike weight. Heavier loads need more pressure to hold the same tire shape.
* Tire width. Wider tires carry the same load at lower pressure.

Tire casing, tubed or tubeless setup, and rim width also change the result. Wider rims spread the tire and lower the pressure needed.

## Road bikes

Road tires are usually 23 to 32 mm wide. Narrow tires need higher pressure.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 70 kg (150 lb) on dry pavement:

* 23 mm: about 100 to 120 psi (6.9 to 8.3 bar)
* 25 mm: about 90 to 110 psi (6.2 to 7.6 bar)
* 28 mm: about 80 to 100 psi (5.5 to 6.9 bar)
* 32 mm: about 65 to 85 psi (4.5 to 5.9 bar)

Adjust from there:

* Heavier riders or loaded bikes: add 5 to 10 psi.
* Lighter riders: subtract 5 to 10 psi.
* Wet or rough roads: drop 5 to 10 psi for more grip and comfort.
* Tubeless setups: most riders can run 5 to 10 psi lower than tubed setups with the same tire.

Road tires lose pressure slowly. Check before each ride, because a tire that is 10 psi low feels soft and slows you down.

## Gravel bikes

Gravel tires are usually 35 to 50 mm wide. Gravel riding mixes pavement, dirt, loose stone and mud, so grip and puncture protection matter more than top speed. Lower pressure works well here.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 70 kg (150 lb):

* 35 to 40 mm, tubed: about 40 to 50 psi (2.8 to 3.4 bar)
* 35 to 40 mm, tubeless: about 30 to 40 psi (2.1 to 2.8 bar)
* 42 to 50 mm, tubeless: about 25 to 35 psi (1.7 to 2.4 bar)

Adjust from there:

* Smooth gravel or mostly pavement: use the higher end of the range.
* Loose, rocky or corrugated gravel: drop 3 to 5 psi.
* Heavier riders or loaded bags: add 3 to 5 psi.
* Pinch flats or rim dents: raise the pressure by 2 to 3 psi.

For tubeless gravel setups, sealant and a secure bead help the tire hold lower pressure without burping air.

## Mountain bikes

Mountain tires are usually 2.2 to 2.6 inches wide, and some trail tires reach 2.8 inches. Most riders run tubeless. Trail terrain varies widely, so pressure is mostly a matter of feel and trial.

Starting ranges for a rider of about 70 kg (150 lb), tubeless:

* 2.2 to 2.3 inch, cross country: about 25 to 30 psi (1.7 to 2.1 bar)
* 2.3 to 2.5 inch, trail: about 22 to 27 psi (1.5 to 1.9 bar)
* 2.5 to 2.6 inch, trail or enduro: about 20 to 25 psi (1.4 to 1.7 bar)
* Downhill or heavy enduro: often 18 to 23 psi (1.2 to 1.6 bar)

Tubed mountain tires need more pressure, usually 30 to 40 psi (2.1 to 2.8 bar), to avoid pinch flats.

Adjust from there:

* Heavier riders: add 2 to 3 psi.
* Lighter riders: subtract 2 to 3 psi.
* Rocky, rooty or fast descents: drop 2 to 3 psi for more traction and impact absorption.
* Smooth, fast trails or hard-pack: raise 1 to 2 psi for less rolling resistance.
* Pinch flats or rim damage: raise the pressure in small steps.

When you first lower pressure, the tire may sit close to the rim. Check that the bead is seated and the rim is not touching the ground.

## How to set and check pressure

* Use a gauge. Pumps with built-in gauges are often off by several psi, so a separate gauge is more reliable.
* Check cold. Measure before riding, because riding warms the air and raises pressure.
* Temperature changes pressure. Pressure rises about 1 psi for every 10 F (about 6 C) of warming and falls as the air cools.
* Note the setting. Once you find a pressure you like, write it on the frame or in a note. Re-check after each change in weather or terrain.
* Stay within the sidewall limit. Never exceed the maximum printed on the tire, and do not inflate a tubeless tire beyond the rim maximum without seating it safely.

## Quick troubleshooting

* Squirming or sliding in corners: pressure is too low, or the tire is too wide for the rim. Raise pressure a few psi.
* Pinch flats: pressure is too low for the impact, or the rider is heavy for the setup. Raise pressure a few psi.
* Harsh or bouncy ride: pressure is too high. Lower it a few psi.
* Tubeless tire not sealing: the bead may not be seated or the sealant may be low. Check the bead and add sealant before adjusting pressure.

## Summary

* Road: 80 to 120 psi, depending on width and load.
* Gravel: 25 to 50 psi, depending on width, setup and surface.
* Mountain: 20 to 30 psi tubeless, with higher pressures for tubed tires and heavy loads.

Use these numbers as a starting point, then adjust in small steps until the tire grips, rolls and resists pinch flats for your riding.

# Tire Pressure Guide: Road, Gravel and Mountain Bikes

Tire pressure affects grip, rolling speed, comfort, and how often you get pinch flats. The right number depends on your weight, the tire width, the surface, and your riding style. Start with the ranges below, then adjust by feel.

## How pressure works

Lower pressure lets the tire deform around bumps, which increases grip and comfort. It also increases rolling resistance on smooth pavement if it is too low, and it raises the risk of pinch flats and rim damage on hard hits. Higher pressure rolls faster on smooth surfaces but feels harsh and skids more easily on loose or wet ground.

Three factors set the starting point:

- **Rider and bike weight.** Heavier loads need more pressure to support them.
- **Tire width.** Wider tires run at lower pressure for the same support.
- **Surface.** Rough, loose, or wet ground calls for lower pressure.

## Road bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 23 to 32 mm.

**Typical pressure range:**

| Tire width | Rider about 60 to 75 kg (130 to 165 lb) | Rider about 75 to 90 kg (165 to 200 lb) |
|---|---|---|
| 23 mm | 100 to 110 psi (6.9 to 7.6 bar) | 105 to 115 psi (7.2 to 7.9 bar) |
| 25 mm | 90 to 100 psi (6.2 to 6.9 bar) | 95 to 105 psi (6.6 to 7.2 bar) |
| 28 mm | 80 to 90 psi (5.5 to 6.2 bar) | 85 to 95 psi (5.9 to 6.6 bar) |
| 32 mm | 65 to 80 psi (4.5 to 5.5 bar) | 75 to 85 psi (5.2 to 5.9 bar) |

**Notes:**

- Check the sidewall. The maximum pressure printed there is a safety limit, not a target.
- Tubeless road tires often run 5 to 10 psi lower than the same tire with a tube.
- Wet roads and rough chipseal call for the lower end of the range.

**Signs you are off:** Pressure too high gives a jarring ride, and the tire skips over small cracks. Pressure too low gives a squirmy feel in corners, a soft or rolling tire under hard pedaling, and frequent pinch flats.

## Gravel bikes

**Typical tire widths:** 35 to 50 mm.

**Typical pressure range:**

| Tire width | Rider about 60 to 75 kg (130 to 165 lb) | Rider about 75 to 90 kg (165 to 200 lb) |
|---|---|---|
| 35 mm | 35 to 45 psi (2.4 to 3.1 bar) | 40 to 50 psi (2.8 to 3.4 bar) |
| 40 mm | 30 to 40 psi (2.1 to 2.8 bar) | 35 to 45 psi (2.4 to 3.1 bar) |
| 45 mm | 28 to 36 psi (1.9 to 2.5 bar) | 32 to 40 psi (2.2 to 2.8 bar) |
